one_liner: Formally verified C/asm crypto library; its ADX X25519 took about 4% fewer cycles than OpenSSL's ADX assembly.
what_it_does: HACL* is a library of verified primitives (X25519, Ed25519, AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305, SHA-2/3, HMAC, HKDF and more). They are written in F*/Low* and Vale and shipped as generated C and assembly in dist/. For X25519, EverCrypt_Curve25519.h exposes secret_to_public, scalarmult and ecdh, which all take caller-allocated 32-byte buffers. At run time it picks one of two back-ends: portable radix-51 C (Hacl_Curve25519_51) or C plus Vale x86-64 assembly (Hacl_Curve25519_64). It is a raw-primitive API, not an OpenSSL replacement: there is no EVP, key-format or TLS layer.
how_it_is_fast: The fast back-end does field arithmetic mod 2^255-19 in radix-2^64 (four limbs) with Vale-verified x86-64 assembly. The assembly uses MULX (BMI2) and the two independent carry chains ADCX/ADOX (ADX), following Oliveira et al.'s ADX Curve25519. It adds fused fmul2/fsqr2 routines that multiply or square two field elements in one call. The Low* Montgomery ladder is specialised for clamped scalars: it starts with bit 254 set, runs 251 steps over bits 253..3 and ends with three doublings, which reduces conditional swaps. The paper credits these changes with beating Oliveira et al. by about 1%.
when_to_use: X25519 key exchange (TLS 1.3, WireGuard/Noise, HPKE) on x86-64 CPUs with both BMI2 and ADX, when you want machine-checked memory safety, functional correctness and secret-independent timing without losing speed to hand-written ADX assembly.
C projects that can vendor a few generated .c/.S files (EverCrypt_Curve25519, Hacl_Curve25519_51/64, AutoConfig2, Vale cpuid and curve25519 asm, karamel headers) instead of linking all of libcrypto.
Mixed fleets that ship one binary: EverCrypt_Curve25519 checks CPUID at run time and uses the ADX path only where it is supported.

Kernel or other freestanding-style code: Linux carries a derivative (lib/crypto/x86/curve25519.h, copyright INRIA, CMU and Microsoft). When it replaced the previous ADX code, Donenfeld measured it within about 1.6% either way of that code on 10 Intel CPUs.
when_not_to_use: Raw speed is your only reason to switch. The measured gain over OpenSSL is about 4% on one Kaby Lake CPU against a 2018-19 OpenSSL build, and in the kernel tests it roughly ties the fastest unverified ADX code.

CPUs without ADX (for example Haswell, which has BMI2 only) and non-x86 targets. These fall back to portable radix-51 C, which Figure 9 puts at 135,636 cycles, about 14% slower than OpenSSL's ADX assembly (118,604). configure excludes Hacl_Curve25519_64.c on anything other than x64.
You need a TLS stack, the EVP interface, PEM/DER key handling or certificates. This repo provides primitives only.

Assuming the other primitives also beat OpenSSL. The paper says only that AES-GCM and ChaCha-Poly 'meet or exceed' OpenSSL. In its picoquic test, EverCrypt's ChaCha20-Poly1305 was slower (84.3 vs 90.9 MB/s).

You want versioned, supported C releases. The README calls this the research home and points production users to cryspen/hacl-packages, which was last pushed in April 2025. Changing the code itself needs F*, Z3, KaRaMeL and Vale.

integration.dependencies: No F*/Z3 needed to use dist/. You need the KaRaMeL runtime headers (dist/karamel) and Hacl_Krmllib. EverCrypt dispatch also needs EverCrypt_AutoConfig2.c and the Vale cpuid-x86_64-*.S. The fast path needs curve25519-x86_64-*.S or the GCC inline-asm header curve25519-inline.h. config.h is generated by dist/configure. The dist Makefile can build libevercrypt.a/.so.
integration.min_toolchain: C11 GCC/Clang for gcc-compatible (it uses VLAs; the Makefile passes -std=gnu11). MSVC needs the msvc-compatible dist, which uses external .asm instead of inline asm. configure disables addcarry intrinsics on GCC < 5.5 (bug 81300) and inline asm on one broken Apple clang build. The paper benchmarked with GCC 7.3.
integration.platforms: Fast path: x86-64 with BMI2+ADX, with Linux, macOS, MinGW and MSVC assembly variants. Everywhere else, portable radix-51 C (best with 64-bit __int128; 32-bit uses emulated 128-bit arithmetic). configure also handles aarch64, ARMv7, s390x, ppc64le and x86.
integration.thread_safety: Not documented. From the code: the Curve25519 functions keep all state in stack buffers, so they should be reentrant. EverCrypt_AutoConfig2_init writes unsynchronized global CPU-feature flags, so call it once before starting threads.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — it replaces OpenSSL only at the raw X25519 primitive (scalarmult/ecdh on 32-byte buffers); there is no EVP_PKEY, BIO or libssl-compatible interface

gotchas: Call EverCrypt_AutoConfig2_init() before anything else. Otherwise the BMI2/ADX flags stay false and EverCrypt_Curve25519_* silently runs the slow portable path; the docs say skipping init means always getting the fallback.
Dispatch requires both BMI2 and ADX. A BMI2-only CPU such as Haswell gets the portable code; the Linux commit notes that 'haswell no longer benefits'.

ecdh returns false when the shared secret is all zeros (low-order peer key), so check the result; scalarmult does no such check. Clamping is implicit: the ladder reads only bits 3-253 and treats bit 254 as set. Open issue #1071, an unreviewed LLM audit, notes that the F* spec never calls decodeScalar.

The proofs trust F*, Z3, KaRaMeL, the C compiler and the inline-asm constraint strings. In 2021, imprecise clobber annotations in the Vale Curve25519 inline asm caused trouble with old GCC in the kernel (PR #501). NULL arguments are unchecked preconditions, not defensive checks (issue #327).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over msotoodeh/curve25519 when you want proven correctness and constant-time guarantees for X25519, not just an unverified speed-tuned implementation. Pick AWS-LC or wolfSSL instead when you need a full TLS library with an OpenSSL-style API rather than a vendored primitive.
verified_claims_summary: Figure 9 of the IEEE S&P 2020 EverCrypt paper was measured on an Intel Kaby Lake i7-7560 with GCC 7.3 -O3 -march=native, with Hyper-Threading and Turbo off. EverCrypt's Low*+Vale X25519 took 113,614 cycles per scalar multiplication against 118,604 for OpenSSL's ADX assembly (commit e8fb288): about 4.2% fewer cycles, and about 1% fewer than Oliveira et al. (115,122). The other implementations ran in-kernel under kbench9000, but OpenSSL ran the 'same script' in user space, and the public kbench9000 x25519 branch has no OpenSSL harness.
status_note: The research repo is actively maintained (last main commit 2026-04-10; Apache-2.0, with the generated C also MIT) and dist/ is easy to copy, but there are no versioned C releases, and the README sends production users to cryspen/hacl-packages, itself last pushed in April 2025.
